scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, I'm engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. My mom is really excited about going wedding dress shopping with me and has booked an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. But here's the thing: I don't want a white dress, and that shop only does white bridal dresses. I already looked it up, so I know that's their thing. I think the whole white wedding dress thing is kind of stupid. It started with Queen Victoria, right? It's not some ancient tradition. Plus, the idea that white symbolizes purity, innocence, or virginity is outdated and doesn't really make sense to me anymore. I mean, why should the color of my dress define my worth or my marital status? But the main reason I'm against a white wedding dress is personal. My mom wore a white dress when she got married, and now she's divorced. Every other woman in my family has worn a colored dressâĢĶusually blue or red, either really pale or really dark. And guess what? They've all had long, mostly happy marriages, some even till death did them part. So, seeing that pattern, I feel like colored dresses might bring better luck or something. When my mom asked why I didn't want a white dress, I first gave her the Queen Victoria line, but she said that wasn't enough justification. Then I mentioned that I'm not exactly "innocent," which was an awful conversation to have with my mom. She got upset, and when she said that wasn't good enough, I finally admitted that her being the only one to break the tradition and also the only one to get divorced didn't exactly instill confidence in white dresses. My mom got really quiet, and I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologized yet, but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the three perfectly fine answers I'd given before that. I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with because it's my wedding, and the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiancÃ©. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first three answers I gave, then I wouldn't be in this situation. So, is it AITA (Ask If There's Anything) for me to tell my mom that she's the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things: 1. **Communication Styles**: How did I communicate my reasons to my mom? Was it respectful, or did it come off as blaming her for my decision? 2. **Family Dynamics**: How does my mom feel about the divorce? How does she feel about traditions? How does she feel about my wedding choices? 3. **Personal Boundaries**: Is it okay for me to make decisions about my wedding without feeling pressured by family traditions or past family events? 4. **Emotional Impact**: How did my mom react when I told her? Did I consider her feelings when I made that statement? 5. **Traditions vs. Personal Choice**: Is it fair to associate the color of the dress with the success of a marriage? How much weight should traditions hold in personal decisions? 6. **Resolution**: How can I resolve this situation to maintain a good relationship with my mom while still making choices that feel right for me? I think it's important to approach this with empathy. My mom went through a divorce, and bringing that up in the context of my wedding choices might have been hurtful. Even though I have valid reasons for wanting a colored dress, the way I expressed it might have made her feel like I'm blaming her for my decision. On the other hand, it's also important for me to feel confident and happy in my choices. I shouldn't feel pressured to conform to traditions or past events that don't align with how I want to celebrate my marriage. Maybe a better approach would have been to express my preference for a colored dress without tying it directly to her past experiences. I could have focused on the aspects of the dress that I like, how it fits my personality, and how it aligns with my vision for the wedding. It's also worth considering having a conversation with my mom to apologize for how I made her feel and to explain my reasons in a way that doesn't place blame on her. This could help mend the relationship and ensure that both of us feel respected and heard. In the end, it's a balance between respecting family traditions and honoring personal preferences. It's okay to have different opinions, and it's important to communicate them in a way that fosters understanding rather than conflict.
